summary: Proposes conventions for using an IBM 2741 typewriter-style terminal to log in to ARPANET server hosts. The 2741 can key in 92 different codes, but a few of them, such as the cent sign and the new-line key, have no direct ASCII equivalent, so the note suggests how to map them. RFC 135 responded with a different set of conventions.

eli5.summary: A special typewriter has a few keys that other computers do not understand. This note decides what those keys should turn into, like agreeing that a smiley key means a colon and a bracket.

subtitle: How to type every ASCII character from a typewriter-style IBM 2741 terminal when logging in to ARPANET server hosts.

tldr.problem: An IBM 2741 terminal can key only 92 codes, so it cannot key all 128 ASCII codes that server hosts expect: 7 ASCII graphics and 31 ASCII controls are missing, and its cent sign and New Line key have no ASCII code.
tldr.mechanism: The note picks one escape character and a few single-character functions, then defines escape pairs that stand in for each missing graphic and control code.
tldr.outcome: It is a proposed set of conventions, not a standard. The unit metadata lists RFC 135 as an update to it.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 135 as an update to this note, and gives its status as unknown. The RFC itself is a set of recommended conventions from March 1971.

sections.title: The 2741 Terminal Problem
sections.content:
An IBM 2741 terminal can key in 92 different codes: 88 graphics plus four controls, SP, BS, HT and NL. Each of these has a defined ASCII code except the cent graphic and the New Line control.

When NL is keyed, the program receiving the keyboard input can translate it into whichever line end the host in use needs: NL, CR or LF.
sections.eli5: The special typewriter has fewer keys than the language computers use. A few of its keys do not match anything, so we need a plan.

sections.title: What Must Be Keyable
sections.content:
Seven ASCII graphics ({ } [ ] ^ \ `) and 31 ASCII controls cannot be keyed on a 2741. To reach all 128 ASCII codes, one character must be chosen as an escape (prefix) character that, together with the characters after it, converts into any desired ASCII code.

Three other functions are usually a single key: character delete (removes this character and the one before it), line delete (removes this character and all earlier ones on the line) and logical line end (treated as if NL were entered, so one physical line can hold several logical lines).

The note also wants a system escape character, so that keyed text can be read by the user program instead of being sent to the Server Host. The same user program may need to send the INS or INR network control commands, either after the system escape or through the 2741 'attention' button, depending on the user's operating system.
sections.eli5: We need one secret key that says the next letters mean something special, plus keys for erasing a letter, erasing a line, and ending a thought early.

sections.title: Recommended Special Characters
sections.content:
The note recommends these characters for the special functions. Because the cent sign and the logical NOT sign are not in ASCII, the text writes them as $CENT and $NOT.

  • Character escape: $NOT
  • System escape: |
  • Character delete: @
  • Line delete: $CENT
  • Logical line end: the # sign

The system escape also lets a user give other commands to the user program, such as suppressing or restoring typeout of received messages, sending received messages or keyed input to a disk file, or aborting the user program.
sections.eli5: The note hands out jobs to keys: one key is the secret prefix, one erases a letter, one erases a line, and one talks to your own computer instead of the far one.

sections.title: Escape Pairs for Missing Codes
sections.content:
For the seven missing ASCII graphics, the character escape plus one key is recommended: $NOT < gives [, $NOT > gives ], $NOT ( gives {, $NOT ) gives }, $NOT " gives ^, $NOT / gives \ and $NOT ' gives `.

The special function characters themselves can be keyed the same way, for example $NOT - for $NOT and $NOT : for |.

ASCII controls use the character escape followed by two letters taken from the control's mnemonic, for example $NOT BE for BEL (X'07') and $NOT ES for ESC (X'1B'). The controls SP, BS and HT can be keyed either way.
sections.eli5: To type a missing symbol, press the secret key and then a stand-in key. For a missing control, press the secret key and two letters that spell its name.

items.label: Character escape
items.desc: Prefix that turns the next characters into any ASCII code.

items.label: System escape
items.desc: Lets keyed text go to the user program instead of the host.

items.label: Character delete
items.desc: Deletes this and the preceding character.

items.label: Line delete
items.desc: Deletes this and all previous characters in the line.

items.label: Logical line end
items.desc: Ends a logical line as if NL were entered.
